question.title: Kubernetes Engine Overview
question.scenario: A company wants to run containerized microservices with automatic scaling, load balancing, and self-healing capabilities without managing the Kubernetes control plane.
question.question-text: Which GCP service provides a managed Kubernetes environment for deploying containerized applications?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Look for GCP's managed Kubernetes service that handles the control plane for you while still giving you full access to Kubernetes APIs for orchestrating containerized workloads.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Google Kubernetes Engine (GKE) is a managed Kubernetes service that simplifies container orchestration at scale. Google manages the control plane (API server, etcd, scheduler, controller manager), automatic upgrades, and cluster health monitoring while you focus on deploying and managing your applications through standard Kubernetes APIs. App Engine Flexible runs containers but abstracts away Kubernetes entirely, offering no access to Kubernetes concepts like pods, services, or deployments. Cloud Run is serverless container execution with no cluster management but also no Kubernetes API access. Compute Engine provides raw VMs where you would need to install and manage Kubernetes yourself. Only GKE provides a managed Kubernetes environment.

ul.li: GKE Autopilot mode fully manages the entire cluster including nodes, removing the need to configure machine types, node pools, or scaling policies. You pay per pod resource request rather than per node, making cost management simpler and eliminating idle node waste.

GKE Standard mode gives you control over node configuration, machine types, and node pool settings, which is useful when workloads have specific hardware requirements like GPUs, high memory, or local SSDs.

Workload Identity links Kubernetes service accounts to GCP IAM service accounts, providing a secure and auditable way for pods to access GCP services without managing service account keys or storing credentials in secrets.

GKE integrates with the full GCP DevOps toolchain: Cloud Build for CI, Artifact Registry for container images, Cloud Deploy for managed continuous delivery, and Binary Authorization for enforcing that only trusted container images are deployed to clusters.

question.title: Cloud Operations Suite
question.scenario: An operations team needs to monitor application performance, collect logs, trace requests across microservices, and receive alerts when issues occur.
question.question-text: Which GCP offering provides integrated monitoring, logging, and application performance management?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Look for GCP's integrated observability platform (formerly called Stackdriver) that bundles monitoring, logging, tracing, error reporting, and alerting into a single unified suite.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Cloud Operations Suite (formerly Stackdriver) is an integrated set of tools for monitoring, logging, and observability across GCP and hybrid/multi-cloud environments. It includes Cloud Monitoring for metrics, dashboards, and uptime checks; Cloud Logging for log aggregation and analysis; Cloud Trace for distributed request tracing; and Error Reporting for exception tracking. Cloud Console is the web-based management UI for GCP resources, not an observability platform. Cloud Debugger was a tool for inspecting application state in production (now deprecated), not a comprehensive monitoring suite. Cloud Scheduler is a managed cron job service for scheduling tasks. Only Cloud Operations Suite provides the integrated monitoring, logging, tracing, and alerting described in the scenario.

ul.li: Cloud Monitoring supports over 1,500 built-in metrics from GCP services, custom metrics from your applications, and uptime checks that monitor endpoint availability from multiple global locations. Dashboards are fully customizable and can be defined as code using JSON or Terraform.

Cloud Logging provides centralized log management with log-based metrics (extracting numeric metrics from log entries), log routing (sending logs to different destinations based on filters), and log sinks that export to Cloud Storage, BigQuery, or Pub/Sub for long-term analysis and compliance retention.

Cloud Trace collects latency data from distributed applications, showing the full request path across microservices with timing breakdowns at each hop. This is essential for identifying performance bottlenecks in microservices architectures like the one described in the scenario.

Alerting policies combine metric conditions (threshold, absence, or rate-of-change) with notification channels (email, SMS, PagerDuty, Slack, Pub/Sub, or webhooks). Policies support multi-condition logic, allowing alerts that fire only when multiple conditions are simultaneously true to reduce alert noise.

question.title: Cloud Console and CLI
question.scenario: A new GCP user needs to manage their cloud resources using both graphical and command-line interfaces.
question.question-text: What are the two primary interfaces for managing GCP resources?

choices.choice: Cloud Console (web UI) and gcloud CLI

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Think about the two primary management interfaces Google provides: a web-based graphical console and an installable command-line tool that together cover interactive and scriptable resource management.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: The Cloud Console is a web-based graphical interface for managing GCP resources with dashboards, forms, and visualizations, ideal for exploration and visual management. The gcloud CLI is a command-line tool for scripting, automation, and efficient resource management from any terminal. Both can manage the same resources and are the two primary interfaces Google provides. SSH is a protocol for connecting to Linux VMs, not a GCP management interface. FTP is a file transfer protocol with no GCP management capabilities. REST APIs underlie all interfaces but are not a primary user-facing management tool (they are used by the console, CLI, and client libraries internally). Terraform is a third-party IaC tool, not a Google-provided primary management interface.

ul.li: Cloud Console includes Cloud Shell for terminal access directly in the browser, providing immediate gcloud CLI access without local installation. It also includes the Cloud Shell Editor (web-based IDE) for editing configuration files and code alongside terminal commands.

The gcloud CLI is part of the Google Cloud SDK, which also includes gsutil (Cloud Storage operations), bq (BigQuery operations), and kubectl (Kubernetes operations). Together these specialized tools cover the most common GCP management tasks from the command line.

Client libraries for Python, Java, Go, Node.js, C#, Ruby, and PHP provide programmatic access to GCP services for building applications that interact with cloud resources. These libraries call the same REST/gRPC APIs that the Console and gcloud use under the hood.

Infrastructure as Code tools like Terraform (multi-cloud) and Config Connector (Kubernetes-native) enable declarative resource management through version-controlled configuration files. While not primary interfaces, they are the recommended approach for managing production infrastructure reproducibly.

question.title: Shared VPC
question.scenario: An organization has multiple projects that need to share a common network infrastructure while maintaining separate billing and IAM for each project.
question.question-text: Which GCP feature allows multiple projects to use a common VPC network managed by a host project?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Think about the GCP networking feature that designates one project as the network owner (host) and lets other projects (service projects) deploy resources into the shared network while keeping their own billing and IAM.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Shared VPC allows an organization to connect resources from multiple service projects to a common VPC network owned by a host project. This enables centralized network administration (firewall rules, subnets, routes managed in one place) while each project maintains separate billing, IAM, and resource management. VPN Gateway creates encrypted tunnels to external networks, not shared internal networks across projects. VPC Peering connects two separate VPC networks for private communication, but each project still manages its own network independently without centralized control. Cloud Router handles BGP routing between your VPC and external networks. Only Shared VPC provides the centralized host-project network model with service project resource deployment.

ul.li: The host project owns the Shared VPC network, subnets, firewall rules, routes, and VPN/Interconnect connections. Network administrators in the host project control all networking configuration centrally, ensuring consistent security policies and IP address management across the organization.

Service projects contain the actual workload resources (VMs, GKE clusters, Cloud SQL instances) that use subnets from the shared network. Subnet-level IAM permissions control which service projects can deploy resources into which subnets, enabling network segmentation by environment or team.

A key difference between Shared VPC and VPC Peering: Shared VPC provides a single shared network with centralized management, while VPC Peering connects two independent VPC networks that are each managed separately. Shared VPC is preferred when you want one team to control all networking; VPC Peering is preferred when teams need independent network management.

Shared VPC works within a single organization. The host project and all service projects must belong to the same GCP organization. Cross-organization network sharing requires VPC Peering or Cloud VPN. Shared VPC supports up to 1,000 service projects per host project.

question.title: Container Registry and Artifact Registry
question.scenario: A development team needs a secure place to store and manage their Docker container images for deployment to GKE.
question.question-text: Which GCP service provides a managed repository for storing container images and other artifacts?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Look for GCP's managed artifact repository service that stores Docker container images alongside other package formats, with built-in vulnerability scanning and IAM-based access control.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Artifact Registry is a fully managed, private repository for storing container images and language packages (Maven, npm, Python, Go, and more). It provides IAM-based access control, automatic vulnerability scanning to identify CVEs in container images, and tight integration with CI/CD tools like Cloud Build. Cloud Build is a CI/CD platform that builds and tests code, but it stores artifacts in Artifact Registry, not within itself. Cloud Storage is generic object storage; while Container Registry historically stored images in Cloud Storage buckets behind the scenes, Cloud Storage itself is not a container registry. Source Repositories hosts Git source code, not built container images. Only Artifact Registry provides the dedicated artifact repository with container-specific features the scenario needs.

ul.li: Artifact Registry replaced the legacy Container Registry, adding support for multiple artifact formats beyond Docker images. New projects should always use Artifact Registry. Existing Container Registry users should migrate, as Container Registry is in maintenance mode.

Automatic vulnerability scanning (via Container Analysis) identifies known CVEs in container images when they are pushed to the registry. It continuously monitors for newly discovered vulnerabilities in previously scanned images and can be combined with Binary Authorization to block deployment of images with critical vulnerabilities.

Remote repositories cache packages from public registries (Docker Hub, Maven Central, npm, PyPI) within your Artifact Registry, providing faster builds, reducing external dependency on public registries, and creating an audit trail of which external packages are used in your organization.

Virtual repositories aggregate multiple underlying repositories (standard and remote) behind a single endpoint, simplifying client configuration. Developers configure a single repository URL, and Artifact Registry resolves packages from the correct underlying repository based on configurable priority rules.

question.title: Private Google Access
question.scenario: VMs without external IP addresses need to access Google APIs like Cloud Storage and BigQuery without routing traffic through the public internet.
question.question-text: Which feature allows VMs with only internal IPs to reach Google APIs and services?

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Think about the subnet-level feature that enables VMs with only internal IP addresses to reach Google APIs and services through internal routing, without needing external IP addresses or Cloud NAT.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: Private Google Access allows VMs with only internal IP addresses to reach Google APIs and services (Cloud Storage, BigQuery, Container Registry, etc.) using internal routing rather than the public internet. It is enabled at the subnet level and works transparently with no changes to application code or DNS. Cloud VPN creates encrypted tunnels to on-premises or other cloud networks, not to Google APIs. Cloud NAT provides general outbound internet access for private VMs, but Private Google Access is more efficient and specific for reaching Google services because traffic stays on Google's internal network. VPC Peering connects two VPC networks together, not VMs to Google APIs. Only Private Google Access provides the direct internal path to Google services for private VMs.

ul.li: Private Google Access is enabled per-subnet in the VPC configuration. When enabled, VMs in that subnet can reach Google API endpoints (like storage.googleapis.com) using their internal IP as the source address, with traffic routed through Google's internal network rather than the public internet.

Private Service Connect takes this further by creating private endpoints (internal IP addresses) within your VPC for Google APIs and services. Instead of accessing public API endpoints, your applications connect to a private IP in your VPC, providing even more control over routing and DNS resolution.

Cloud NAT and Private Google Access serve different purposes and can coexist: Private Google Access handles traffic to Google APIs, while Cloud NAT handles traffic to the general internet. A VM with Private Google Access enabled can reach Cloud Storage without Cloud NAT, but needs Cloud NAT to reach external websites like GitHub or package registries.

On-premises hosts can access Google APIs privately through Cloud VPN or Cloud Interconnect combined with Private Google Access. This enables hybrid architectures where on-premises applications securely access GCP services like BigQuery or Cloud Storage without exposing traffic to the public internet.

question.title: GCP Free Tier
question.scenario: A student wants to learn GCP without incurring costs, using free resources for small-scale projects and experimentation.
question.question-text: What does GCP's Free Tier provide to new users?

choices.choice: Free credits only for certified professionals
$300 credit for 90 days plus always-free tier resources
Free access only during business hours
Unlimited free access to all services for one year

hint.label: Brief Hint
hint.content: Think about the two components of GCP's Free Tier: a time-limited credit for trying any service, plus a set of always-free product quotas that never expire and are available to all accounts.

hint.label: Complete Explanation
hint.content: GCP's Free Tier includes two components: $300 in credits valid for 90 days that new users can spend on any GCP service to explore the platform, plus Always Free tier products that provide limited free usage of certain services indefinitely (no expiration). Option A is wrong because the free trial is available to anyone, not just certified professionals. Option C is wrong because there are no time-of-day restrictions on free tier access. Option D is wrong because access is limited by credit amount and specific service quotas, not unlimited, and the Always Free tier has no one-year expiration. Only option B correctly describes both the $300/90-day trial and the perpetual Always Free resources.

ul.li: Always Free products include: 1 e2-micro VM instance (in select US regions), 5 GB of Cloud Storage (regional, Standard class), 1 GB of Firestore storage with 50K reads/20K writes/20K deletes per day, and 10 GB of BigQuery storage with 1 TB of queries per month. These quotas reset monthly and never expire.

Cloud Functions provides 2 million invocations, 400,000 GB-seconds of compute time, and 200,000 GHz-seconds of CPU time per month for free. Cloud Run provides 2 million requests, 360,000 GB-seconds of memory, and 180,000 vCPU-seconds per month for free. These serverless free tiers are generous enough for learning and small production workloads.

During the 90-day free trial, GCP will not charge your credit card even if you exceed the $300 credit; resources are simply shut down. After the trial, you must explicitly upgrade to a paid account to continue using resources beyond the Always Free quotas, preventing surprise charges for students and learners.

Budget alerts should be set up even on free tier accounts to monitor spending against the $300 credit and to provide early warning if Always Free quotas are being approached after the trial ends. The combination of free tier resources and billing alerts makes GCP accessible for learning without financial risk.
